EVs are a lot better than ICEVs Internal Combustion Engine Vehicles (ICEV) Electric Vehicles (EV) Winner Major Components IC engine, Transmission System. DC/AC motor, digital controller, battery pack. Image Credits EV PMF IAS – Learn Smart 39 Weight Comparatively heavier. Comparatively lighter. EV Heavy due to large and heavy metallic engines with complicated design. Motor engines are relatively lighter as they have fewer components and simplistic design. EV Space occupied by components Comparatively more because of large engines. Comparatively less Î more space for seating Î good for congested countries like India EV Efficiency Less efficient because of loss of energy in the form of heat in IC engines and due to friction between transmission systems (rotatory motion has to be transmitted using a complex set of bearings and shafts). More efficient as the loss of energy in the form of heat is very low (not many moving parts in motors) and transmission losses are minimum (the motor engine shaft transmits rotatory motion either directly to the wheels or with the help of fewer bearings and shafts). EV Maintainance More maintenance (frequent, oil change, components replacement) is required as there are many moving parts. Less maintenance as the battery is the only major component to be replaced. (low recurring cost) EV The initial cost of development and ownership Comparatively low as the technology is in place for a century now. High as the technology is still evolving. IC Total lifecycle economic cost High Low (electricity cost associated with operating an EV over a distance of 1 km is significantly lower than the petrol/diesel cost required to operate a comparable IC vehicle) EV Acceleration and speed control Comparatively less as there many states like ignition, four stages of IC engine, transmission, etc. EVs are much faster as the transmission of power, and rotatory motion is almost instanta- neous. EV Environmental footprint High Comparatively low (EV are more efficient) Range Once the tank is full ICEVs can travel non-stop for hundreds of km The range of EVs at present is only a few hun- dred km. Battery capacity is increasing, and prices are falling x Lithium-Ion batteries are increasing in energy density at a rate of 5-8% per annum. x Battery Costs are falling: The main cost of an electric vehicle is the cost of the battery. Lithium-Ion batteries cost $1,000 per kWh in 2010. By 2017 that cost had fallen to $200 per kWh, and it won't stop there. Favourable policy x China and India are aggressively pushing for electric mobility with a slew of measures. x India reduced GST on EVs from 12% to 5%. Introduced schemes like FAME, FAME II. Economies of EV PMF IAS – Learn Smart 41 x NITI Aayog has proposed to ban all IC (internal combustion) engine powered two-wheelers (below 150cc) and three-wheelers in India starting in 2025 for two-wheelers and in 2023 for three-wheelers. x The automobile industry had objected to the proposal as EVs are still not financially viable. The battery pack takes up nearly half the cost of an average electric vehicle x For EVs to be viable, the cost of battery packs needs to reduce significantly. x The predominant battery chemistry used in EVs is lithium-ion batteries (Li-ion). x The key-components of the battery contribute the most (60%) to the total cost. x Labour charges, overheads and profit margins account for the rest. x Any reduction in the cost of the battery pack will have to come from a reduction in battery materials cost. Can costs be further decreased? x The price of Li-ion battery packs has consistently fallen over the past few years. x This decrease is in part due to technological improvements, economies of scale and increased demand. x Given that raw materials account for 60% of the cost of the battery pack, the room for further cost reduction is limited. What does it mean to India? x India needs to manufacture Li-ion cells in-house and recycle existing Li-on batteries to bring down costs. x However, the government has not taken any significant steps in this direction. Nanoparticles x A Nanoparticle is a small particle that ranges between 1 to 100 nanometres (nm) in size. x Undetectable by the human eye, nanoparticles can exhibit significantly different physical & chemical properties to their larger material counterparts. x Nanoparticles (NPs) have wide variety of potential applications in the fields of biomedical, optical & elec- tronics research. What is Nanotechnology? x Nanotechnology is science, engineering, & technology conducted at the nanoscale (1 to 100 nanometres). x Nanoscience & nanotechnology can be used across all the other science fields. Gold Nano Particles (GNP) PMF IAS – Learn Smart 42 x Gold Nano Particles (GNP) are a small gold particle with a diameter of 1 to 100nm which, once dispersed in water, are also known as colloidal gold. x The versatile surface chemistry of gold nanoparticles allows them to be coated with small molecules, poly- mers, & biological recognition molecules, thereby extending their range of application. x The morphology of gold nanoparticles is spherical, & they appear as a brown powder. Applications of Gold Nano Particles (GNP) x GNPs can be used as a composite therapeutic agent clinical trials, especially in Anti–cancer, Anti–Viral, anti– diabetic, & cholesterol–lowering drugs. x Researchers have coated gold particles with DNA & injected them into plant embryos or plant cells. This will ensure that some genetic material will enter the cells & enhances plant plastids. x Gold nanoparticles are used to detect breast cancer. x Photodynamic therapy: when light is applied to a tumour containing gold nanoparticles, the particles rap- idly heat up, killing tumour cells. x It was also discovered that the nanoparticles could detect toxins & pathogens. x The scattered colours of gold nanoparticles are currently used for biological imaging applications. x The optical–electronics properties of gold nanoparticles are being explored widely for use in high technol- ogy applications. Param Siddhi Supercomputer x It is the-high performance computing-artificial intelligence (HPC-AI) supercomputer established under National Supercomputing Mission (NSM) at C-DAC. x The supercomputer has Rpeak of 5.267 Petaflops and 4.6 Petaflops Rmax. x Rmax and Rpeak are scores used to rank supercomputers based on their performance. National Supercomputing Mission (NSM) x NSM was set up to provide the country with supercomputing infrastructure by manufacturing supercomput- ers indigenously in India. x NSM is steered jointly by the 9 Ministry of Electronics and IT (MeitY) and 9 Department of Science and Technology (DST). PMF IAS – Learn Smart 43 x It is implemented by the 9 Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC), Pune and 9 Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bengaluru. x The target of the mission was set to establish a network of supercomputers ranging from a few Tera Flops to greater than or equal to 3 Peta Flops (PF) in institutions of National importance across the country by 2022. x This network of Supercomputers envisaging a total of 15-20 PF was approved in 2015 and was later revised to a total of 45 PF (45000 TFs). x Supercomputer PARAM 8000 (made by C-DAC) launched on July 1, 1991 is considered India's first super- computer. It was indigenously built in 1991 by C-DAC. x National Supercomputing Mission's first indigenously build supercomputer is called ‘Param Shivay’ x Param Shivay was followed by Param Shakti and Param Brahma supercomputers. Focus of the mission x The Mission envisages empowering national academic and R&D institutions spread over the country by in- stalling a vast supercomputing grid comprising of more than 70 high-performance computing facilities. x These supercomputers will also be networked on the National Supercomputing grid over the National Knowledge Network (NKN). x The NKN is another programme of the government which connects academic institutions and R&D labs over a high speed network. Significance of supercomputers x Most to the supercomputers across the world are dedicated for weather and climate research. x Weather prediction has reached accuracy of forecast as well as real time tracking of natural phenomenon. x Timely warning of cyclones in the recent past have saved many lives and property. The speed of a Supercomputer x The average computer’s processor performance is measured by megahertz (MHz) units to calculate its clock speed. x Since supercomputers are far more capable, the performance is calculated in Floating-point operations per second, or FLOPS which is of a considerably larger scale. Ö 1 billion flops = 1 giga flops (109) Ö 1000 giga flop = 1 tera flop (1012) PMF IAS – Learn Smart 44 Ö 1000 tera flop = 1 peta flop (1015) x Param 8000 supercomputer had a maximum speed of one giga flop. x PARAM SHIVAY (February 2019) Î 833 TFLOPS x PARAM Brahma (September 2019) Î 0.85 PFLOPS x Pratyush and Mihir (fastest supercomputers in India) Î 6.8 PetaFlops x The most advanced supercomputer Summit (U.S.) Î ~150 PFLOPS. Reverse osmosis (RO) x NGT has recently passed an order prohibiting the use of reverse osmosis (RO) purifiers where total dissolved solids (TDS) in the supplied water are below 500 mg per litre. x The NGT had ordered the ban on the grounds that RO filters often deprived drinking water of essential salts (affecting the nutritional security) and were also wasting a lot of water and power. x Current BIS regulations consider 500 mg/litre to 1,200 mg/litre of total dissolved solids, which consist of salts and some organic matter, as acceptable. x MoEF has recently issued a draft notification that seeks to regulate membrane-based RO water filtration systems in areas where the source of water meets drinking water norms of the Bureau of Indian Standards. Basics Solution x In chemistry, a solution is homogeneous mixture composed of two or more substances. x In such a mixture, a solute is a substance dissolved in another substance, known as a solvent. x For example, in salt water, salt is the solute and water is the solvent. Diffusion x Diffusion is a spontaneous movement of a substance from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration. PMF IAS – Learn Smart 45 x Diffusion through a permeable membrane moves a substance (solute) from a region of high solute concen- tration (hypertonic solution) to a region where its concentration is low (hypotonic solution).
